title: Learn the HTTP Protocol in Go
description: Implement HTTP from raw TCP streams through requests, responses, chunked bodies, trailers, and binary data.

lessons.title: Welcome to 'Learn the HTTP Protocol'
lessons.instruction: HTTP/1.1 is structured bytes carried by a reliable stream. Build the smallest valid request by correcting its request target; the CRLF boundaries are already visible in the program.

lessons.title: TheStartup™
lessons.instruction: The project boundary is simple: connection bytes enter a parser, and a handler eventually produces response bytes. Mark the parser component ready for the first checkpoint.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	component := "parser"
	state := "TODO"
	fmt.Println(component, state)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	component := "parser"
	state := "ready"
	fmt.Println(component, state)
}

lessons.title: 8 Bytes
lessons.instruction: A read buffer is not a message boundary. Read may fill only part of an eight-byte buffer, so append buf[:n], never the unused or stale bytes after n.

lessons.title: Newlines
lessons.instruction: HTTP/1.1 lines end with CRLF, not a lone newline. Two consecutive CRLF sequences form the empty line that separates headers from the body.

lessons.title: Channel Refactor
lessons.instruction: A channel can carry ordered read chunks between a producer and parser. The consumer must range until the producer closes the channel or it will silently discard later chunks.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	chunks := make(chan string, 3)
	chunks <- "GET "
	chunks <- "/items "
	chunks <- "HTTP/1.1"
	close(chunks)
	fmt.Println(<-chunks)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	chunks := make(chan string, 3)
	chunks <- "GET "
	chunks <- "/items "
	chunks <- "HTTP/1.1"
	close(chunks)
	var message string
	for chunk := range chunks {
		message += chunk
	}
	fmt.Println(message)
}

lessons.title: TCP
lessons.instruction: TCP is an ordered, reliable byte stream without application message boundaries. Use net.Pipe to observe that one write may require multiple reads by the receiver.

lessons.title: TCP vs. UDP
lessons.instruction: TCP exposes a connection-oriented stream. UDP preserves individual datagrams but does not guarantee their arrival or order. Correct the transport descriptions.

lessons.title: UDP Sender
lessons.instruction: A UDP write sends one datagram to one address. Prepare the destination and payload without contacting an external service; the address and bytes are enough for this checkpoint.

lessons.title: Files vs. Network
lessons.instruction: Network reads can be short even when more bytes will arrive. Treat every io.Reader as incremental and loop until framing or EOF instead of trusting one Read call.

lessons.title: TCP to HTTP
lessons.instruction: HTTP turns TCP bytes into messages by defining delimiters and lengths. Remove the complete CRLF delimiter from the first line, not just its final newline byte.

lessons.title: The RFCs
lessons.instruction: RFC 9110 defines HTTP semantics. RFC 9112 defines HTTP/1.1 message syntax and connection handling. Keep those roles straight when an edge case is unclear.

lessons.title: HTTP Post
lessons.instruction: A POST body begins after the empty header line. Content-Length is the body length in bytes, so derive it from the actual payload before building the raw request.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	body := "hello"
	raw := fmt.Sprintf("POST /notes HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Length: %d\r\n\r\n%s", 4, body)
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", raw)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	body := "hello"
	raw := fmt.Sprintf("POST /notes HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Length: %d\r\n\r\n%s", len([]byte(body)), body)
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", raw)
}

lessons.title: cURL
lessons.instruction: A curl command makes a request reproducible. Use -X for the method, -H for the media type, and --data for the body in the required order.

lessons.title: Testing With Testify
lessons.instruction: Assertion helpers improve failure messages, but the important part is a table containing valid and malformed request lines. Tighten valid so all three cases pass.

lessons.title: Parsing the Request Line
lessons.instruction: An HTTP/1.1 request line is method, request-target, and version separated by single spaces. Assign each parsed field to its correct role.

lessons.title: Parsing a Stream
lessons.instruction: A parser must return both the completed line and every byte already read after its CRLF. Preserve that remainder for the header parser.

lessons.title: Request Line Review
lessons.instruction: Reject missing fields, extra fields, and unsupported versions instead of accepting a convenient prefix. Repair the validator used by this compact review.

lessons.title: State Machine
lessons.instruction: Incremental parsing is easier to reason about with explicit states. Transition at each space, then require CR followed by LF to finish the request line.

lessons.title: Connect the Parsing
lessons.instruction: The connection reader may split a request line anywhere. Accumulate fragments before searching for CRLF so the parser sees a continuous stream.

lessons.title: Headers
lessons.instruction: Header names are case-insensitive. Use Go's http.Header instead of a plain case-sensitive map so Content-Type and content-type identify the same field.

lessons.title: Constraints
lessons.instruction: A field name cannot contain spaces, and whitespace before the colon is invalid. Tighten the validator so only the correctly formed header is accepted.

lessons.title: Multiple Values
lessons.instruction: Repeated fields must be preserved. Header.Set replaces existing values, while Header.Add appends another value under the canonicalized field name.

lessons.title: Add to Parse
lessons.instruction: After the request line, parse header lines until the first empty line. Do not treat the body or later bytes as more headers.

lessons.title: Live Headers
lessons.instruction: A field line can be split between any two bytes, including CR and LF. Join the received fragments before parsing complete lines.

lessons.title: Parsing the Body
lessons.instruction: Content-Length is a decimal byte count. Read exactly that many bytes; trailing bytes can belong to another message on the same connection.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	length := 5
	buffer := []byte("helloextra")
	body := buffer
	fmt.Printf("%d %s\n", length, body)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	length := 5
	buffer := []byte("helloextra")
	body := buffer[:length]
	fmt.Printf("%d %s\n", length, body)
}

lessons.title: Live Body
lessons.instruction: Body bytes may arrive over several reads. Stop at the declared length and retain any surplus bytes instead of consuming the start of the next message.

lessons.title: Body Review
lessons.instruction: A body is complete only when available bytes equal its declared length. Fewer bytes are incomplete; more bytes leave a remainder for later parsing.

lessons.title: Server
lessons.instruction: A server owns each accepted connection until its response is written or an error ends the exchange. Use net.Pipe to return a successful status line locally.

lessons.title: Content Length
lessons.instruction: Content-Length counts encoded bytes, not Unicode code points. Measure the UTF-8 body as bytes so a client reads the complete representation.

lessons.title: Response
lessons.instruction: An HTTP/1.1 response is a status line, header fields, an empty CRLF line, then the body. Insert the missing empty line before the payload.

lessons.title: Other Common Headers
lessons.instruction: Content-Type describes the representation and Connection can describe connection handling. Set values that match this JSON response and its deliberate close behavior.

lessons.title: Handler
lessons.instruction: Keep application decisions separate from wire serialization. Implement the health route as a small handler that returns a status and body.

lessons.title: Code Review
lessons.instruction: io.Writer may accept fewer bytes than requested. Review the response write and loop until every byte is committed instead of silently truncating the status line.

lessons.title: Refactor
lessons.instruction: Centralize response framing so every handler gets the same CRLF and byte-length rules. Replace the ad hoc output with one small response helper.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	body := "created"
	raw := "HTTP/1.1 201 Created\r\n" + body
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", raw)
}

lessons.title: Chunked Encoding
lessons.instruction: Each chunk begins with a hexadecimal size, followed by CRLF, that many data bytes, and another CRLF. Parse the size in base sixteen until the zero chunk.

lessons.title: Chunked Quiz 1
lessons.instruction: Chunk-size uses hexadecimal notation. Decode 1f with base sixteen rather than treating it as an ordinary decimal number.

lessons.title: Chunked Quiz 2
lessons.instruction: Chunk metadata and data can both cross read boundaries. Reassemble the fragments before decoding the complete four-byte chunk.

lessons.title: Chunked Quiz 3
lessons.instruction: Transfer-Encoding: chunked frames the body independently of Content-Length. Honor chunked framing first and stop only at its zero-size chunk.

lessons.title: Trailers
lessons.instruction: Trailer fields follow the zero chunk and end at another empty line. Continue parsing after the zero-size line so allowed metadata is not discarded.

lessons.title: Binary Data
lessons.instruction: An HTTP body is arbitrary bytes, not necessarily valid text. Preserve NUL and invalid UTF-8 bytes and inspect them without converting the payload to a human string.

lessons.title: HTTP 2 and 3
lessons.instruction: HTTP semantics remain familiar while framing changes: HTTP/1.1 is textual, HTTP/2 multiplexes binary frames over TCP, and HTTP/3 carries frames over QUIC.
